presentingComplaint: Severe constant epigastric pain radiating to the back for 10 hours with repeated vomiting
history: Known alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, prior variceal banding, on propranolol and spironolactone) with ongoing heavy alcohol use, admitted after 10 hours of severe boring epigastric pain radiating to the back, worse lying flat and relieved by sitting forward, with persistent bilious vomiting and inability to tolerate oral intake. He binged on spirits over the preceding two days. No haematemesis or melaena. No prior similar episodes. The overlap with his liver disease is deliberate and confounding: he has known ascites and baseline mild jaundice, and his coagulopathy and hypoalbuminaemia are chronic, so standard severity indices are muddied. However, the acute, dynamic epigastric-to-back pain with vomiting and a lipase greater than three times the upper limit of normal points clearly to acute pancreatitis superimposed on cirrhosis.
examination: Ill-looking, mildly icteric, dehydrated with dry mucous membranes. Abdomen distended with shifting dullness consistent with pre-existing ascites, with marked epigastric tenderness and voluntary guarding but no rebound; bowel sounds sluggish. Spider naevi and palmar erythema noted. No flank or periumbilical ecchymosis. No asterixis; orientated to time, place and person.
imaging: Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen (performed at 72h for severity): diffusely enlarged, oedematous pancreas with peripancreatic fat stranding and acute peripancreatic fluid collections, no established necrosis (CT Severity Index moderate). Coarse nodular liver with splenomegaly, recanalised paraumbilical vein and moderate ascites consistent with cirrhosis with portal hypertension. No gallstones or biliary dilatation; no free air.
microbiology: Blood cultures drawn for fever sent and pending; diagnostic ascitic tap performed to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis showed ascitic neutrophils <250/mm3 (no SBP). No antimicrobials indicated for sterile pancreatic inflammation.
finalDiagnosis: Acute (alcohol-induced) pancreatitis in a patient with alcohol-related cirrhosis - diagnosis by 2 of 3 revised Atlanta criteria (characteristic pain + lipase >3x ULN, corroborated by CT)
citations: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) - Guidelines for the Management of Acute Pancreatitis, 2024
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Acute and Chronic Pancreatitis
stewardship: Non-infective diagnosis: acute pancreatitis is a sterile inflammatory process and prophylactic antibiotics are NOT indicated even in moderately severe disease or sterile peripancreatic collections (ACG 2024). Management is supportive: goal-directed isotonic crystalloid resuscitation (with caution for the hypoalbuminaemic cirrhotic to avoid worsening ascites/overload), analgesia, antiemetics, early enteral nutrition as tolerated, correction of hypocalcaemia, and treatment of the alcohol withdrawal risk. Antibiotics are reserved only for a proven or strongly suspected superimposed infection (e.g., infected necrosis, cholangitis, or SBP), none of which is present here. Ascitic tap was appropriately performed to exclude SBP given the cirrhosis and mild fever.
contraindications: Avoid aggressive high-volume fluid boluses given cirrhosis with ascites/hypoalbuminaemia - titrate to perfusion, not fixed large volumes
Avoid NSAIDs for analgesia (renal impairment, portal-hypertensive GI mucosa, coagulopathy)
Avoid empiric/prophylactic antibiotics for sterile pancreatitis
Caution with sedating opioids given borderline hepatic encephalopathy risk
edgeCases: Chronic hypoalbuminaemia, thrombocytopenia and elevated INR from cirrhosis can falsely inflate pancreatitis severity scores (e.g., BISAP/APACHE) - interpret against the patient's baseline
Pre-existing cirrhotic ascites can be mistaken for pancreatic fluid collection or masked SBP - a diagnostic tap is essential
Lipase can be mildly elevated in renal impairment; the >3x ULN threshold with concordant imaging keeps the diagnosis secure
Baseline jaundice from cirrhosis must not be over-attributed to biliary obstruction - no biliary dilatation on CT argues against cholangitis
expectedMaiK: Diagnose acute pancreatitis using the revised Atlanta criteria (characteristic epigastric-to-back pain plus lipase/amylase >3x ULN) and recognise that antibiotics are not indicated for sterile pancreatitis; provide supportive care with fluids titrated cautiously in a cirrhotic patient, while distinguishing pancreatic pathology from decompensated cirrhosis, variceal/peptic bleeding and biliary sepsis.

Any haematemesis, melaena or change in stool colour

expectedInvestigations: Transabdominal ultrasound to look for gallstones/biliary dilatation

Diagnostic ascitic tap to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

investigations: Diagnostic ascitic tap to exclude SBP

regressionAssertions: Engine must return pancreatitis as the top diagnosis
Engine must NOT recommend prophylactic antibiotics for sterile acute pancreatitis
Severity scoring must be interpreted against cirrhotic baseline (chronic low albumin, thrombocytopenia, raised INR)
